What is the dot com crash?

I had a crush job as a web programmer. Had a Mohawk and wore a hoodie to work. Why? Because I could. We had a giant warehouse space in San Francisco, no cubicles, totally open. Foosball table, nba jams and mortal kombat 3 arcade machines. We hosted parties, rented out tiki lounges, lived opulently. There was a lot of money being tossed around in the 90's. "THE INTERNET" was the billion dollar wave of the future and everyone was throwing money at every startup company they could find in hopes something would stick. We made a lot of legit websites, but what paid the bills was porn. We had an award winning (AVN) website. Our corporate customers didn't know about that part though. Anyway, so about the bubble bursting. People (investors) began to realize the money they threw at startups wasn't making them anything. Dotcom businesses were being propped up by more and more VC cash that was disappearing into the void or up people's noses. The great swollen beast of wealth was really festering inside. So there was a panic as investors realized they were wasting money on the huge gambles. They pulled out the money, most of the Dotcom businesses fails in short order. I shaved my Mohawk, put on a tie and got a fucken job.
Such an awesome way of describing it.

Basically, after the Internet launched in 1991, there was an enormous surge in investment in Internet companies. Investors were fascinated by the opportunities the shiny, newfangled technology offered, so online businesses could count on receive enormous investment, regardless of how economically feasible they really were. Investors just blindly bought up stocks of Internet companies due to massive hype and catchy names rather than a viable business plan. Eventually, investors caught on that just because a company was online, it didn't automatically make it profitable. Investment dried up, and many online companies rapidly lost tons of money. Then, the whole thing came crashing down. Hundreds of companies were forced to shut down or declare bankruptcy.
